extracted.intended_audience: scientists, experimentalists, and students of scientific method/philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and standards for discovering causal laws by observation and experiment (Mill's account of varying circumstances, the Method of Agreement and the Method of Difference), including limitations of pure observation and advantages of artificial experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varying the circumstances (Baconian rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the Baconian rule of varying the circumstances: to determine which antecedents are connected with which consequents we must be able to meet with some antecedents apart from the rest, or some consequents apart, and observe what follows from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundation of experimental inquiry. To assign cause to effect we must either find instances in nature where antecedents occur separately or artificially arrange circumstances so antecedents can be isolated. Varying circumstances enables us to discover which concomitants are essential and which are casual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement — FIRST CANON
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more instances of the phenomenon under investigation have only one circumstance in common, the circumstance in which alone all the instances agree, is the cause (or effect) of the given phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare different instances of a phenomenon; whatever circumstance is invariably present across diverse instances is indicated as connected with the phenomenon. Examples: combination of oil and alkali producing soap; crystallization following deposition from a liquid. Limitation: finding an invariable antecedent by agreement does not by itself prove unconditional causation unless the antecedent can be shown (ideally by experiment) to produce the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference — SECOND CANON
rubrics_metrics.description: If an instance in which the phenomenon under investigation occurs, and an instance in which it does not occur, have every circumstance in common save one, that one occurring only in the former; the circumstance in which alone the two instances differ, is the effect, or the cause, or an indispensable part of the cause, of the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare an occurrence and a non-occurrence that are identical except for a single factor. This method is especially powerful in artificial experiments where one can ensure the two instances differ only in the presence/absence of the candidate cause. It more directly establishes causation than Agreement when its strict similarity condition is met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Elimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental inquiry proceeds by successive exclusion of the various circumstances accompanying a phenomenon to ascertain which can be absent and which cannot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both Agreement and Difference are elimination methods: Agreement shows what can be eliminated (hence not connected), Difference shows what cannot be eliminated (hence connected). Use systematic exclusion to narrow down causes/effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentation enables control and production of needed variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial experiment extends observation by producing combinations and particular sorts of variation that nature rarely offers, enabling precise study of a phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: isolating atmospheric gases to discover oxygen supports respiration; electric machines and batteries reveal electrical phenomena invisible in storms. Experiments let us choose concomitant circumstances and introduce well-defined changes to observe resultant effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation alone can ascertain sequences and co-existences but cannot by itself prove causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation (purely finding instances in nature) can show invariable antecedence or co-existence but cannot establish unconditional causation unless the antecedent can be produced and the effect observed following it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without producing the antecedent under known conditions (reverse test), an invariable antecedence might be due to a common underlying cause (e.g., day and night). Observation is essential where experiment is impossible, but its conclusions about causation remain provisional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversibility/Production test to confirm causation
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish that an invariable antecedent is truly the cause, one should reverse the proof by producing the antecedent artificially and observing whether the effect follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The addition of experimental evidence (producing A and observing a) converts invariable antecedence into causal knowledge. Historical examples: artificially producing crystals from silica-laden water or producing marble by cooling fused materials under pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insulation of the phenomenon among known circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: When we can produce a phenomenon, we should place it among known circumstances so that we know exactly what else is present, and then observe what alteration its introduction makes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This isolation permits subsequent stepwise variation of circumstances and clearer attribution of observed changes to the introduced factor. It reduces unknown concomitants that would confound interpretation in spontaneous natural cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of near-identical instances for Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: The two instances compared in the Method of Difference must resemble one another in every respect except the presence or absence of the phenomenon (or antecedent) under investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This strict similarity is usually unattainable in spontaneous natural occurrences due to complexity and unobserved factors, but is achievable in controlled experiments where one definite change is introduced rapidly into a known pre-existing state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement is applicable when controlled experiments are impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement does not require specially prepared pairs of instances; any natural instances showing the phenomenon can be compared to detect common antecedents or consequents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Agreement in domains where experiment is impracticable (e.g., astronomy, many aspects of social/psychological phenomena), recognizing that Agreement may identify invariable concomitants but not necessarily causal relations without additional evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical decomposition: mental analysis precedes physical separation
rubrics_metrics.description: The observer must mentally decompose complex phenomena into constituent antecedents and consequents before attempting physical separation or experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good observation is an intellectual skill: noticing components, discriminating relevant circumstances, and avoiding confounding imagination with observation. Training (self-education) rather than a formal 'art of observing' is needed to prepare the mind to observe productively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stepwise introduction of well-defined circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce one well-defined circumstance after another into an experimental setup to determine how the phenomenon behaves under varied conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chemists and experimentalists apply additives, heat, pressure, electricity etc., one at a time to see specific interactions and dependencies. This clarifies the range and limits of a phenomenon's behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations from unascertainable or multitudinous concomitants
rubrics_metrics.description: In many natural or complex systems (e.g., human minds, societies), the multitude and unobservability of concomitant circumstances render direct experimental methods impracticable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases induction from direct experience is at a severe disadvantage and methods of the science must rely more on deduction or different approaches; be cautious about assigning causal status in presence of many unknown factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical distinction: Difference suits artificial experiment, Agreement suits observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Method of Difference is primarily a method of artificial experiment because it needs precise instance-pairs; Method of Agreement is mainly used where experimentation is impossible and relies on comparing varied natural instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the method appropriate to the practical constraints of the subject matter: use Difference when you can control and rapidly change circumstances; use Agreement when you must rely on naturally occurring variations.
